cards.front: What does unary mean for an operator?
cards.back: It takes one operand — binary takes two, ternary takes three
cards.extra: The unary group in Java is ++x, x++, --x, x--, unary + and -, bitwise complement ~ and logical NOT !. "Unary" counts operands, not characters — it is unrelated to the number one as a value.
cards.example:
-x     !ready     ~bits     i++
// each operator here has exactly one operand

cards.front: What does the unary ~ operator do to an integer?
cards.back: Flips every bit — for an int it is the same as -x - 1
cards.extra: It works on integral types only, never on boolean (that is !). Flipping all bits of 5 gives -6 in two's complement; ~0 is -1 and ~-1 is 0.
cards.example:
int x = 5;
System.out.println(~x);   // -6

cards.front: Which direction does a chain of ternary operators group?
cards.back: Right to left — a ? b : c ? d : e is a ? b : (c ? d : e)
cards.extra: JLS 15.25 says the conditional operator is syntactically right-associative. The dev.java table mentions only assignment as right-to-left, but the ternary is too; assignment is separately right-to-left (a = b = 5 is a = (b = 5)).
cards.example:
boolean t = true, f = false;
String s = t ? "A" : f ? "B" : "C";  // "A"

cards.extra: Multiplicative (*, /, %) sits one level above additive (+, -). Same-level operators run left to right, which is why 10 / 2 * 5 is 25, not 1.
cards.example:
int a = 2 + 3 * 4;   // 14, not 20
int b = 10 / 2 * 5;  // 25

cards.extra: Shifts (<<, >>, >>>) sit below additive and above relational. 1 << 3 + 2 gives 32, because the addition happens first and 3 + 2 becomes the shift distance.
cards.example:
int a = 1 + 2 << 3;   // (1+2) << 3 = 24
int b = 1 << 3 + 2;   // 1 << (3+2) = 32
